items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Blue wave = a cap on the dollar, not a trend change, if the AI trade is the dollar's hidden bid
items.idea: Innes argues the dollar's recent strength leaned on global capital chasing US tech, so the AI selloff already leaked into JPY/CHF. Prediction markets had ~74% on a Democratic Senate. His line: political scrutiny is not an investment cycle 'brought to its knees', and the Fed reaction function still sets USD.
items.angle: The unspoken link: if AI capex is the marginal USD buyer, a Congress hostile to data centers hits FX via capital flows, not via fiscal. Watch USDJPY and DXY against SOX, not against the election map.
items.tweetA: Everyone is debating whether the Democrats are bearish for the dollar. Wrong variable. The dollar's marginal buyer in 2026 is a hyperscaler's capex budget. Trade DXY against SOX, not against the Senate map.
items.tweetB: 5-week low in DXY, gold +2.8%, 74% Senate odds already in the price. If this is a 'political' dollar move it fades by Friday. If it's an AI-flows move, it doesn't. Which one are you positioned for?

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: RBA hikes to 4.85% on a 6–3 vote and deletes its tightening bias: 'hike but lose the argument'
items.idea: RBA delivered the expected hike to 4.85% but split 6-3, removed the reference to further tightening for the first time since June, and downgraded the outlook on falling house prices and rising unemployment risk. Markets now price only ~1-in-3 odds of another hike and 13bp of easing by end-2027. AUD still carries the best vol-adjusted yield in G10.
items.angle: A central bank hiking into falling house prices is the late-cycle signature. Pair it with the ECB still leaning hawkish: the dispersion trade is who blinks first.
items.tweetA: RBA hiked and the currency fell. That's what a policy mistake looks like in real time: the hike is priced, the guidance is the news, and the guidance just got deleted. Falling house prices do the rest.
items.tweetB: AUD has the best carry in G10 and a central bank that just took the next hike off the table. Carry works until vol collects the rent. With the AI complex shaking out, the rent is due.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: French spreads stuck above 150bp even as Brent falls below $105
items.idea: Innes notes OAT spreads have stayed above 150bp despite the retreat in oil, so the market is demanding political/fiscal premium independent of energy. EUR/USD sits near 1.12 with the ECB still leaning toward at least one more hike.
items.angle: If oil falling doesn't compress OAT-Bund, the premium is structural, and a hawkish ECB is tightening into a sovereign spread that won't close. Links to the 'Paris burning' aside in Noahpinion.
items.tweetA: Brent down, OAT-Bund still >150bp. The spread isn't about energy anymore. An ECB hiking into that is tightening against its own weakest sovereign.
items.tweetB: Euro bulls want a weaker dollar. Fine. But EUR/USD at 1.12 with France at +150bp is a currency pricing the dollar's problem and ignoring its own.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Nasdaq futures were -2% on election night, then went green: 'buy before, buy after, buy the mess'
items.idea: Nasdaq futures fell more than 2% on the sweep, the dollar dropped and Treasuries bid, then equity futures recovered into positive territory. Since 1970 the S&P has averaged +14.1% in the six months after midterms vs +5.7% in other years, and every post-midterm six-month window was positive.
items.angle: A 100% hit rate on a sample of ~14 is a seasonal, not a law, and this cycle has an AI financing problem the sample never had. But the shakeout-and-recover pattern is consistent with positioning being already light.
items.tweetA: S&P +14.1% in the six months after midterms since 1970, positive every single time. Sample size: about 14. Good seasonal, bad religion. What's different this time is the AI financing question, not the election.
items.tweetB: Nasdaq futures went from -2% to green in a few hours on the biggest political shock of the year. When bad news can't hold a bid down, the sellers were already gone. That's the signal, not the 1970 stat.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: 'A war launched to force regime change in Iran ended up delivering regime change in Washington'
items.idea: Innes frames the midterm sweep as blowback from the Iran war and its gas-price shock. Related: the oil price move (Brent ~$95-105) and Boockvar/Noah Smith both tie voter anger to inflation and gasoline above $4 on Election Day.
items.angle: The political cost of an oil shock is now measurable: $4 gasoline plus a House flip. That changes the incentive to keep the Strait premium alive.
items.tweetA: Gasoline crossed $4 on Election Day and the party in power lost the House 229-139. If you were pricing a long-duration Iran premium in oil, price in the electoral cost of it as well.
items.tweetB: A war for regime change in Tehran; the regime that changed was in Washington. Whatever the next Iran escalation looks like, the White House now has a hard constraint it didn't have a week ago.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Gold's 3.7% Friday plunge was forced liquidation; Bloomberg's White sees bullion below fair value for first time since 2023
items.idea: Innes: Friday's 3.7% drop had forced-selling fingerprints (cash raising against AI equity losses plus CTA momentum selling). Simon White's fundamental model has gold below fair value for the first time since 2023 after a 185% rally. Gold was +3% the next session at ~$4,054.
items.angle: Gold as the first piggy bank raided in stress is the mirror image of its safe-haven story. A valuation reset below model after a 185% run is how bull markets reload.
items.tweetA: Gold fell 3.7% in a day and every macro desk called it a regime change. It was a margin call. Bloomberg's model now has bullion under fair value for the first time since 2023. Forced sellers don't have a view.
items.tweetB: Gold -3.7% Friday, +3% this week, central banks bought 321t in Q3. One of these participants has a price target and it isn't the CTA.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Oil: recovery in Gulf exports and crowded speculative longs complicate the bull narrative
items.idea: Only the preview was in the email body: the piece argues the recovery in Gulf exports and increasingly crowded speculative positioning complicate the bullish oil case. (Body behind the link.)
items.angle: Two-sided oil risk: supply healing from the Gulf vs a crowded long. Compare with Boockvar's 'bull case for oil' the same morning.
items.tweetA: Everyone is long the Hormuz premium. The barrel nobody discusses is the one coming back from the Gulf. Crowded longs and recovering exports is not a bull setup.
items.tweetB: Oil -3% to $95 on the same morning gold rips. When both the hedge and the thing you are hedging against sell off together, the market is telling you about positioning, not supply.

items.title: Intel -30% in a day: ~$140B erased, its worst day ever, -57% from the ATH, despite a Q3 beat
items.idea: INTC lost about 30% at the close, wiping out nearly $140B, the worst collapse in its history. The Q3 numbers beat; the damage came from Q4'26 and Q1'27 commentary. Client and edge revenue is guided down more than 20% sequentially in Q4.
items.angle: A beat-and-collapse on an AI-adjacent name is the same pattern as Gartner/Shopify in the Big Moves list: guidance, not prints, is the trade.
items.tweetA: Intel lost $140B of market cap in one session after beating Q3. Nobody trades the print anymore; they trade the next two quarters of the story.
items.tweetB: Intel is down 57% from its high and the Q3 numbers were good. If a good quarter can't hold a stock, what does that say about stocks priced on perfect guidance?

items.title: Memory prices are now destroying PC demand: Intel sees 2026 PC TAM -12%, H2 units -20%+, 2027 another -10%
items.idea: CFO Zinsner said high memory cost and scarcity forced customers to skip upgrades. 2026 PC unit TAM is -12% with H2 down more than 20%, and 2027 is guided -10% with 'we are not optimistic' on memory and a recovery possibly in H2'27. In Q2, client revenue was up 15% sequentially largely on ASP, not units.
items.angle: The AI memory super-cycle has a victim: consumer compute. Cross-read with Zebra's gross-margin hit from memory and 'memory prices rising into 1H27'.
items.tweetA: AI ate the memory supply, and now Intel says PC units fall -12% this year and -10% next. HBM's winners are conventional DRAM's customers' losers. $MU $INTC $HPQ $DELL
items.tweetB: Q2: Intel client revenue +15% on pricing. Q3: guide down 20%+. The 'strength' was inflation. Rasgon smelled it two quarters early; the rest of the Street read the headline.

items.title: Server CPU upside capped by an EMIB substrate shortage, plus a fatal Fab 28 accident costing ~$600M of revenue
items.idea: Agentic-AI server CPU demand was the bull case, but Lip-Bu Tan said substrate shortages for EMIB packaging stopped Intel shipping as many server CPUs as planned, and Intel 3 yield/cycle times need work. An Oct 14 gas-cylinder explosion at Fab 28 in Kiryat Gat killed two and shut the plant for two weeks: ~$300M hit in Q4 and $300M+ in Q1'27, ~2pt on Q4 gross margin.
items.angle: The bottleneck in the AI buildout keeps migrating: GPUs, HBM, power, now substrates and packaging. Israel single-site concentration is also a geopolitics-adjacent supply-chain risk.
items.tweetA: Demand for server CPUs is there. Intel couldn't ship them because of substrates. The AI bottleneck isn't compute anymore; it's whichever boring input you haven't looked at yet.
items.tweetB: One fab in Kiryat Gat, one accident, $600M of revenue across two quarters. Concentration in a single site in a single geopolitical region is a risk factor, not a footnote.

items.title: Post-mortem: the tell was in Rasgon's Q2 question, client strength was price, not demand
items.idea: Vik walks through how Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon asked in Q2 whether client strength was pricing, got 'largely ASP driven', and followed up in Q3 on memory supply. The lesson is that analysts focused on capex, foundry and ARM competition while the read-through was in the Q&A. Vik states his aim is learning, not bull or bear.
items.angle: A repeatable framework: when revenue is up and units aren't, ask who is paying and for how long. Applies to memory, networking, and AI servers.
items.tweetA: The best signal in Intel's Q2 call was a question, not an answer: 'was it all pricing?' Yes. Revenue up on ASP while the end market softens is a leading indicator everywhere in this cycle.
items.tweetB: Intel's stock death took two earnings calls to telegraph. Which AI names are growing revenue on price right now, and which analyst is asking that question?

items.title: US gas supply growth in 2026 exceeds the entire output of the EU; Appalachian spot is $1-2/MMBtu
items.idea: Doomberg: US natural gas production will grow in 2026 by more than the combined total EU output, and again in 2027. Appalachian spot runs at ~$1-2/MMBtu, or $6-12/bbl oil-equivalent, less than a typical daily Brent swing. EQT agreed to buy Range Resources in a $13B all-stock deal to create the largest US gas producer.
items.angle: Consolidation at trough prices is a bet that LNG plus data-center burn closes the gap. The sign of a cycle bottom, or a value trap if data centers slip.
items.tweetA: US gas production growth in 2026 is bigger than Europe's entire output. At $1-2 gas. Producers are merging at the bottom because they believe in LNG and data centers. One of those two is not guaranteed.
items.tweetB: EQT buying Range for $13B in stock: when the cheapest producers in the world start merging, it's either the bottom or the last chance to get out. $EQT $RRC

items.title: Gas turbine backlog: new orders placed today won't be filled until 2030, some slots are already sold into 2032
items.idea: The gating factor on data-center power is gas turbines. Major suppliers are sold out for years, with reports that new orders land in 2030 and some 2032 slots are being taken. Doomberg notes confidence in data-center demand was shaken by last week's AI equity rout.
items.angle: Turbine makers' backlog is the hardest-to-fake read on whether the buildout is real. Orders for 2032 delivery are made by people who don't plan to blink.
items.tweetA: A turbine ordered today arrives in 2030. Nobody places that order on a whim. Whatever the Nasdaq says about AI, the backlog at the people making the engines is still a seven-year view. $GEV
items.tweetB: Natural gas at $1-2 and no turbines to burn it. The binding constraint on AI isn't the fuel, it's the machine that converts it. That's where the margin is.

items.title: Used aircraft engines as an emergency fix for data-center power: 'flying is about to get more expensive'
items.idea: With turbines scarce, Doomberg points to the tens of thousands of used aircraft engines in service and storage that can be repurposed as power generation, with varying time, effort and cost. The argument is that this arbitrage will tighten the aviation engine aftermarket.
items.angle: A cross-sector squeeze: AI power demand competing with airlines for the same engine pool. Second-order beneficiaries: aftermarket engine lessors and MRO.
items.tweetA: AI's power shortage has reached the airline aftermarket. Data centers are buying jet engines to burn gas. The next AI input-cost story may be in your airfare.
items.tweetB: When the grid can't deliver and turbines are sold out until 2030, people start buying 747 engines. This is what a real shortage looks like. $GE $RTX

items.title: Hedge-fund SMAs hit $255B (+20% y/y); capital is abundant, credible PMs are the scarce asset
items.idea: Goldman puts separately managed hedge-fund accounts at $255B at end-2025, +20% y/y, growing ~13% annually over a decade vs 5.5% for the industry, and links this to talent scarcity. BofA found in September hedge funds raised more capital than planned for the first time in three years, with multi-managers drawing the strongest demand.
items.angle: When capital outruns PM talent, pods start buying talent externally. That raises the correlation of the pod complex and the crowding risk in the same factors.
items.tweetA: Hedge-fund SMAs: $255B, +20% in a year. Capital is not the constraint anymore; a credible PM is. More money chasing the same ~200 people means more crowding in the same trades.
items.tweetB: The multi-manager industry is a talent market that looks like a capital market. SMAs growing 2.4x faster than the industry tell you where the marginal dollar of alpha demand is going.

items.title: Jain Global returns outside capital and manages only for Millennium; Point72 hands Harry Schwefel the president title
items.idea: Bobby Jain launched Jain Global in 2024 with $5.3B, returned 3.7% in 2025, and in April 2026 agreed to return outside capital and manage money exclusively for Millennium. Point72 (~$50B, 3,000+ people) named Harry Schwefel president and created an executive committee while Cohen keeps approval rights. March 2026 was the worst month for global hedge funds since January 2022.
items.angle: Platforms are converting spinouts into SMAs: the 'external pod'. Governance layers appearing at Point72 are the sign a trading shop is becoming an institution.
items.tweetA: Jain left Millennium, raised $5.3B, then handed the capital back to be an external pod for Millennium. The best strategy for a successful PM is to become a vendor to the platform he left.
items.tweetB: Point72 has 3,000 employees and now needs an executive committee under Cohen. At that size alpha is a process problem, not a genius problem. See March 2026: worst month since Jan 2022.

items.title: Texas flips: Abbott loses to Hinojosa, Talarico wins Senate, Kansas, Iowa and South Carolina go blue
items.idea: Noah Smith: Democrats won 'a far more extensive and decisive victory than almost any forecaster anticipated'; even non-college white voters abandoned the GOP. Texas elected a progressive governor and a progressive senator; Ted Cruz is the only statewide Republican left. He cites MAGA primary voters replacing Cornyn with Ken Paxton as part of the cause.
items.angle: A Texas flip matters for the AI buildout: Texas is the center of data-center and gas-fired power plans, and the governor controls permitting and grid policy (ERCOT).
items.tweetA: Texas just elected a Democratic governor. Texas is where the data centers, gas plants and LNG are being built. Re-underwrite every Texas power and AI-infrastructure thesis for a permitting regime change.
items.tweetB: Abbott, a popular incumbent with a strong economy, lost to a progressive. Kansas, Iowa and South Carolina went blue. The polls didn't miss a shy GOP vote, they missed that the swing voters were furious.

charts.desc: Two charts in the email: non-college white vote shift and corruption concern polling

items.title: Corruption beat inflation as voters' top concern: Fox poll 60% 'extremely concerned', WaPo-ABC 2/3 say Trump is enriching himself
items.idea: Noah cites a CNBC survey, a Fox poll (60% of registered voters extremely concerned about government corruption, above inflation), WaPo-ABC-Ipsos (about two-thirds think Trump uses the presidency to enrich himself, +10pt since Sept 2025), Gallup (multi-decade highs) and Reuters/Ipsos (nearly 7 in 10 say his businesses influence decisions).
items.angle: Corruption as the top issue is why crypto-industry ties (WLF) are now a political liability, linking directly to Tiger's read on legislation.
items.tweetA: Corruption passed inflation as the number-one voter issue. That's a very different mandate than 'lower prices', and it lands directly on anything with a Trump-family ticker or token.
items.tweetB: 60% 'extremely concerned' about corruption in a Fox poll. When that number is higher than grocery prices, the 2027 agenda is subpoenas, not stimulus.

charts.desc: Corruption-concern chart from the poll series

items.title: Smith's warning to Democrats: borrowing binge, price controls and billionaire taxes would repeat the mistake
items.idea: Noah lists how Democrats could squander the win: a health-care borrowing binge raising rates, price controls on inflation, billionaire taxes (California's electorate just rejected one), and mass asylum admissions. He says he will write the inverse post in 2030 or 2034 if they do.
items.angle: A split government is the market's favorite thing: no fiscal impulse. The risk is a Democratic House passing messaging bills that pressure term premium anyway.
items.tweetA: The market likes gridlock because it means no new spending. A 54-seat Senate and a House majority is not gridlock in committee rooms: it's subpoena power. Different asset-price implications.
items.tweetB: California just rejected a billionaire tax at the same ballot where Texas flipped. The electorate wants affordability and anti-corruption, not wealth taxes. Whoever reads that wrong loses 2028.

items.source: Danielle DiMartino Booth / The Daily Feather
items.title: S&P Global's monthly GDP: -0.1% in September after -0.6% in August; unchanged activity means Q4 contracts
items.idea: S&P Global's monthly GDP series fell 0.1% in September after a 0.6% decline in August (revised down from -0.2%). The level of September GDP is 1.1% below the Q3 average at an annual rate, so with flat activity in Oct-Dec, Q4 GDP would contract. Only the opening of the note was in the email.
items.angle: A statistical contraction in Q4 sitting beside a Fed debating hikes with oil near $100: stagflation optics ahead of a December meeting.
items.tweetA: S&P Global's monthly GDP has fallen two months in a row. Even if October through December are flat, Q4 prints negative. Meanwhile the debate is about hikes. Pick one.
items.tweetB: -0.6% in August, -0.1% in September, and Q4 negative on a flat run-rate. The Fed is staring at oil; the activity data is staring at a recession.

charts.desc: Fuchsia line: S&P Global monthly GDP level vs Q3 average

items.title: Data-center siting becomes gubernatorial politics: 'counting data centers' state by state
items.idea: Boockvar: the governorship results mean fewer data centers where Democrats won, as threatened on the trail; the question is whether the industry pivots to states that want them. He quotes Comfort Systems: hyperscalers will place bets 'influenced by your perception of whether the Governor in that state wants people to have jobs.'
items.angle: Capex allocation now has a political-geography layer. Winners: states and utilities that court load; losers: the Texas/Virginia premium.
items.tweetA: Hyperscalers don't bet on the grid anymore, they bet on the governor. The next leg of the buildout depends on which state capitals want load. $VRT $ETN $FIX
items.tweetB: Comfort Systems says data-center placement is influenced by whether the governor wants jobs. Every AI capex forecast just got a 50-state political overlay.

items.title: Dollar at a 5-week low, gold +2.8%, S&P futures recovered from -100 to green at 1am ET with no obvious catalyst
items.idea: Boockvar: S&P futures were down ~100 points and started rebounding around 1am ET, which he attributes only loosely to AMD results and election clarity. DXY is at its lowest in 5 weeks, though still in a technical uptrend, and gold is +2.8%, helped by news that central banks want more of it. The Treasury refunding detail came at 8:30am ET.
items.angle: A bounce without a catalyst is a positioning flush. The refunding announcement is the real macro event of the day.
items.tweetA: S&P futures reversed 100 points overnight and the best explanation anyone has is 'clarity'. A move that big with no cause is positioning, and positioning leaves a footprint in the dollar and gold.
items.tweetB: Dollar lowest in 5 weeks, gold +2.8%, the Treasury refunding plan at 8:30. If term premium is going to move on this election, the refunding statement is where it shows.

items.title: 30-year mortgage rate ~7.3%; purchase applications -2% w/w after the first rise in 8 weeks
items.idea: MBA data: average 30-year mortgage rate dipped again to 7.3%, refinancings were flat, and purchase applications fell 2% week over week after rising last week for the first time in eight weeks.
items.angle: A 7.3% mortgage rate with Brent at $95-105 and RBA/ECB hiking: housing is the transmission channel to the Q4 GDP weakness DiMartino Booth flags.
items.tweetA: A 7.3% mortgage rate and purchase apps still falling. The housing market hasn't recovered in 8 weeks of trying. That's the 'higher for longer' bill landing in the real economy.
items.tweetB: Purchases fell 2% as rates dipped. When lower rates can't move volume, it's affordability, not the rate. That's a very different problem for the Fed to solve.

items.source: David Rosenberg / Early Morning with Dave
items.title: Dems 229-139 in the House, 54-44 in the Senate; Dow futures swung from -300 to +500 overnight
items.idea: Rosenberg: polls weren't wrong this time; the Democratic sweep stands at 229-139 in the House and 54-44 in the Senate at last count. Dow futures went from -300 to +500 overnight, an 800-point U-turn; he asks if Texas turning blue can really be good for the data center construction boom. Only the opening takeaway was in the email.
items.angle: He is flagging the same tension as Boockvar: an equity rally that coexists with a policy threat to data-center capex.
items.tweetA: An 800-point round trip in Dow futures on an election result. The market is celebrating gridlock while quietly forgetting that Texas just changed its mind about data centers. $DIA $NVDA
items.tweetB: The market's reflex: 'divided government = bullish'. The footnote: the biggest political change was in the one state building the most AI infrastructure.

items.title: 'How they should trade vs how they actually trade': critical moment for flows, two asymmetric trades on the table
items.idea: Macro Charts says the midterms are over and noise is at a climax; positioning gives a roadmap, 'clean signals are setting up', and he made portfolio changes into two 'extremely asymmetric' opportunities. Only the preview was in the email body; the charts and trades are behind the link.
items.angle: A flows-first view that matches the overnight 100-point reversal: positioning flush rather than news.
items.tweetA: Positioning explains the election-night reversal better than the election does. The clean signal isn't political; it's who was already out.
items.tweetB: Everyone is arguing about what the Democrats will do. The better question is what the asset managers with a record 3M 10-year futures long will do about it.

items.title: Dems hold 54 Senate seats and 228 House seats: Warren, Brown and Waters set to chair crypto committees, CLARITY stalls
items.idea: Tiger Research: with majorities of 54 and 228, critics are likely to chair the committees; Sherrod Brown won despite ~$63M spent by crypto PACs, and Maxine Waters is the likely House Financial Services chair. Republicans Husted and Steil (chair of the digital assets subcommittee) lost. Moderates want conflict-of-interest rules, so the CLARITY Act could be delayed.
items.angle: The legislative upside in crypto is gone for two years; what remains is rulemaking by the SEC/CFTC (which is what the stock-perps story shows).
items.tweetA: Crypto spent $63M to stop Sherrod Brown and he won. The industry didn't just lose a vote; it funded its own opponent's chairmanship. Legislation is dead for two years, rulemaking is all that's left. $COIN $HOOD
items.tweetB: BTC at $78k on a Democratic sweep tells you the market already priced the CLARITY Act as optional. GENIUS is the law. The next 24 months are about the agencies, not Congress.

items.title: First target of a Democratic Congress: World Liberty Financial's 49% stake sold for ~$500M to an Abu Dhabi-linked buyer four days before inauguration
items.idea: Tiger says Democrats have called for Senate hearings on reports that an investor linked to Abu Dhabi's royal family bought 49% of WLF for about $500M four days before Trump's inauguration. Congress is also likely to examine why the SEC dropped more than ten crypto enforcement cases and may delay SEC/CFTC confirmations. Ro Khanna has opened an inquiry into WLF-UAE dealings.
items.angle: Political risk for a Trump-family token has just become subpoena risk. Also ties into Justin Sun's sanctions motion against WLF in the same-day Morning Minute.
items.tweetA: H1 2027 crypto headlines will be subpoenas, not bills. WLF sold 49% to an Abu Dhabi-linked buyer for ~$500M four days before inauguration and Congress now has the gavel. $WLFI
items.tweetB: Justin Sun is asking a court to sanction WLF on the same morning Democrats take Congress. The Trump-family crypto business is being attacked from the left, from the courts, and by its own counterparties.

items.title: Republicans now defend GENIUS with the filibuster and veto; a statutory CBDC ban is dead for two years
items.idea: Tiger: Hagerty and Thompson will shift to defending GENIUS using the 60-vote threshold and veto threat. The Anti-CBDC Surveillance State Act passed the House in July 2025 but stalled in the Senate; Trump's January 2025 executive order is the only explicit federal CBDC prohibition and a future president could reverse it. Attention shifts to Treasury GENIUS rules and stablecoin privacy.
items.angle: CBDC risk shifts from legislative to executive: the 2029 president decides. A stablecoin-privacy fight is the next battlefront.
items.tweetA: The CBDC ban is an executive order, not a law, and the law that would codify it just lost its Senate. Whoever wins 2028 decides whether there's a digital dollar. $USDC $CRCL
items.tweetB: Stablecoin privacy is the sleeper issue: Republicans will scrutinize whether Treasury's GENIUS rules let the government monitor transactions. Circle's $73B of USDC is sitting on that answer.

items.title: CFTC clears stock perps for US trading and Citadel/Cboe-backed group sues the same day
items.idea: CFTC Chair Selig said equity perpetual futures can trade on CFTC-registered exchanges as security futures products. Seven entities hold both CFTC DCM status and SEC notice registration: Cboe, CME, Coinbase, Kalshi, Bitnomial, Nadex and ICE Futures US. Kalshi has filed for 56-58 names with a launch expected within days; Coinbase filed for Apple, Tesla and Nvidia. The Capital Markets Alliance (Cboe, Citadel Securities, Healthy Markets) sued in SDNY arguing these are security-based swaps and that the CFTC violated the APA.
items.angle: 24/7 leveraged single-stock exposure with no expiry, offered by crypto-native venues, is a direct threat to the equity-derivatives incumbents. The lawsuit shows who thinks they lose.
items.tweetA: Citadel Securities sued the CFTC the same day it approved stock perps. When the largest market maker in equities litigates against a product within hours, you know where the margin is. $COIN $HOOD
items.tweetB: Seven firms are registered to list stock perps. Five of them filed inside a single 30-day window in September. This wasn't a surprise approval, it was a coordinated launch.

items.title: Tether says it holds 'give or take 150,000 BTC' but its Q3 attestation shows ~100,100 BTC ($8.37B)
items.idea: At the Plan B Forum in Lugano Ardoino said Tether holds about 150,000 bitcoin, roughly $11.5B at $78.2k. The Q3 attestation accounts for $8.37B of bitcoin, about 100,100 coins, leaving some 50,000 unexplained.
items.angle: A 50% gap between CEO statement and attested holdings is a disclosure question that regulators in a Democratic Congress will ask.
items.tweetA: Tether's CEO says 150,000 BTC. Tether's own attestation says 100,100. The gap is 50,000 coins, ~$3.9B at today's price. Someone will ask which number is right. $USDT
items.tweetB: Tether is now one of the largest BTC holders on the planet by its own account, and the number moves by 50% depending on whether it's a conference or a filing.

items.title: Binance's $6.34B hack: a fake job interview, malware its endpoint tools missed, then weeks of lateral movement using an internal AI tool
items.idea: Binance traced the loss to an engineer asked to download a coding assignment that installed malware; attackers spent weeks moving laterally, abused an internal AI tool to take over two more employees' machines, and reached the wallet signing service on October 29. Maxine Waters cited the hack as proof crypto can't operate without accountability.
items.angle: The attack surface is the hiring funnel plus the company's own AI tooling. It's also political fuel for the committee chair who will oversee crypto.
items.tweetA: $6.34B lost because an engineer did a take-home coding test. The attackers then used Binance's own internal AI tool to hop between machines. Your AI agent is now part of your attack surface.
items.tweetB: Binance, the biggest exchange, was beaten by a fake job interview. Maxine Waters is about to chair the committee that decides what that means for every exchange. $COIN

items.title: GitBook discloses a breach by 'a sophisticated, highly targeted attack using AI agents': tokens, integration secrets and Git Sync keys exposed
items.idea: GitBook disclosed a breach of its infrastructure credentials, describing it as an attack using AI agents, exposing API tokens, integration secrets and Git Sync keys. It comes the same morning as Binance's account of an AI-tool-assisted lateral movement.
items.angle: Two breaches in one newsletter where AI agents were the attack tooling. The cost of sophisticated intrusion just dropped.
items.tweetA: GitBook says it was breached by AI agents. Binance says attackers abused its internal AI tool. Same day. Offensive AI went from a conference talk to a breach report.
items.tweetB: Documentation platforms hold the keys to everyone's repos via Git Sync tokens. Sophisticated, targeted, agentic. The supply-chain attack surface keeps widening.

items.title: Crypto snapshot after the sweep: BTC $78.2k, ETH $2,320, SOL $93, HYPE $84.5, ZEC $1,285; BTC ETFs -$116M, ETH ETFs -$85M
items.idea: Majors were green: BTC +1%, ETH +2%, ZEC +7% at $1,285, LIT +8% after the perps news. Oil -3% to $95; gold +3% to $4,054; Dow futures +1.6%. Bitcoin ETFs saw $116M in outflows Tuesday and ETH ETFs $85M. Hyperliquid led on-chain protocol revenue at $2.07M, ahead of Pump.fun at $1.57M.
items.angle: BTC holding $78k on a bad regulatory night while ETFs bleed means the marginal buyer isn't the ETF channel. ZEC at $1,285 with a private-transactions bid is the standout.
items.tweetA: BTC +1% on the night crypto lost Congress, while spot ETFs saw $116M of outflows. The buyer isn't the ETF channel. ZEC at $1,285 says the market wants privacy more than it wants regulation.
items.tweetB: Hyperliquid, the venue the CFTC just put next in line for approval, leads on-chain protocol revenue. The regulatory regime that kills offshore perps is the same one that crowns the winner.

items.title: Aztec's Tierra upgrade cuts client-side proof time for private transactions to ~1 second; SEC no-action on Canton Coin; NEAR cuts issuance 36%
items.idea: Aztec shipped Tierra, patching a critical vulnerability and cutting proof generation to about one second. The SEC's Corp Fin issued a no-action letter treating Canton Coin as a digital commodity. NEAR's House of Stake voted to cut maximum annual issuance from 2.5% to 1.6% over 24 months. Circle: Q3 revenue and reserve income $865M (+17% y/y), average USDC $73.3B.
items.angle: One-second proofs make private transactions practical; the privacy narrative is going from theory to UX. The no-action letter shows the SEC will still provide clarity via staff.
items.tweetA: Private transaction proofs now take one second. The thing that stopped on-chain privacy wasn't the cryptography, it was the wait. ZEC is not alone in noticing. $ZEC
items.tweetB: The SEC gave Canton Coin a no-action letter while Congress goes hostile. Regulation by staff letter is how crypto actually gets clarity for the next two years.

items.title: Zebra's gross margin falls to 45.7% from 48% on memory costs; management says memory prices keep rising into 1H27
items.idea: Zebra (ZBRA -8.76%) beat on revenue and EPS but gross margin narrowed to 45.7% from 48% a year earlier on higher memory-component costs. Management said memory prices are expected to keep rising into the first half of 2027 despite planned price increases.
items.angle: An industrial-tech name, not a chipmaker, is naming memory as a margin tax into 2027. Cross-read with Intel's PC TAM cut: memory scarcity is hitting end markets broadly.
items.tweetA: Zebra's margin dropped 230bp on memory costs and management sees memory prices rising into 1H27. HBM's boom is a tax on every other device maker. $ZBRA $MU $SNDK
items.tweetB: Intel blames memory for PCs, Zebra blames memory for margins. The AI memory bid is now showing up in the income statements of companies that don't make AI products.

items.title: Consumer trade-down is visible in earnings: K-Cups to instant coffee at KDP, softer restaurant traffic at Sysco
items.idea: Keurig Dr Pepper (-5.65%) beat but cut its legacy-business outlook as consumers shifted from K-Cups to cheaper ground, whole-bean and instant coffee. Sysco (-9.33%) missed on $21.7B revenue and lowered sales guidance to the bottom of 6-7% citing softer restaurant traffic and lower food inflation. Kimberly-Clark closed the ~$48.7B Kenvue acquisition.
items.angle: Trade-down plus $4 gasoline: consumer-staples and food-service volumes are the real-economy confirmation of the housing and GDP softness.
items.tweetA: Americans are switching from K-Cups to instant coffee and eating out less. Combined with $4 gas, the trade-down isn't an anecdote, it's in the guidance of $KDP and $SYY.
items.tweetB: Sysco cut guidance on weak restaurant traffic, Keurig on cheaper coffee. The consumer is voting with a mug. And the election just told you what the consumer thinks about prices.

items.title: AI-infrastructure earnings winners: Lattice +10.98%, Advanced Energy +9.63%, Everus +9.46% on record data-center revenue and expanding backlogs
items.idea: Lattice (record FPGA sales, AI data-center demand, raised outlook), Advanced Energy (record semi-equipment and data-center computing revenue, Q4 above estimates) and Everus Construction (data-center electrical/mechanical growth, higher T&D revenue, expanded backlog, raised FY guidance) all rallied. Talen +7.29% with a $3B repurchase authorization.
items.angle: While Intel collapsed, the picks-and-shovels in power, electrical construction and equipment are posting backlogs and raising guidance. The buildout is rotating down the stack.
items.tweetA: Intel -30%. Lattice +11%, Advanced Energy +10%, Everus +9% on the same tape. The AI trade hasn't broken, it has rotated from the logo to the electrician. $LSCC $AEIS $ECG
items.tweetB: Talen doubled its buyback to $3B with a $1.5B accelerated tranche. When power producers are buying back stock into the AI trade, they're telling you the data-center power contracts are in hand. $TLN

items.title: Apollo -4.95%: $1.06B GAAP loss on marks, spread earnings weak, Athene's alternatives trail target; AUM $1.07T
items.idea: Apollo posted a $1.06B GAAP loss on unrealized mark-to-market adjustments, weaker retirement-services spread earnings, and management conceded Athene's alternative-investment returns trailed the long-term target, even as fee-related earnings rose 23% and AUM hit $1.07T.
items.angle: The private-credit complex is under both a valuation and a redemption squeeze: the same Apollo Debt Solutions fund capped redemptions at 5% for a third quarter.
items.tweetA: Apollo's AUM is $1.07 trillion and it just posted a $1.06B GAAP loss on marks. The mark is the thing everyone pretends is a price. $APO $ARES $BX
items.tweetB: Apollo's insurance arm admits its alternatives trail target, the same week its flagship fund capped redemptions again. The retail-private-credit liquidity promise is being tested in real time.

items.title: Tinder daily actives grow y/y for the first time in ~3.5 years, but payers still fall and Match Group drops 8.5%
items.idea: Match Group (-8.49%) missed on $891M revenue; Tinder revenue and payers kept contracting, Q4 guide flat-to-lower. Yet Tinder DAUs returned to year-over-year growth in September for the first time in about three and a half years, while Hinge grew double digits.
items.angle: Engagement recovering before monetization is the leading indicator of a product turnaround. Gen-Z social-behavior shifts toward in-person dating are a culture signal.
items.tweetA: Tinder DAUs grew year over year for the first time in 3.5 years and the stock fell 8.5%. Usage recovers first, payers follow later. The market is trading the lagging indicator. $MTCH
items.tweetB: Hinge is growing double digits while Tinder payers shrink. The dating market didn't die; it moved to the app that sells intent. $MTCH

items.title: Medicare's WISeR prior-authorization program delays Inspire Medical procedures; revenue -7.9% to $206.7M
items.idea: Inspire (-7.9%) saw US sales decline amid Inspire V coding and reimbursement uncertainty that delayed procedures, including Medicare cases affected by the WISeR prior-authorization program. Vertex fell 4% on Crinetics-related acquisition and integration costs despite revenue above expectations.
items.angle: Prior authorization via a government pilot is a new reimbursement headwind for device makers: regulation affecting medtech volumes before any price change.
items.tweetA: A Medicare prior-auth pilot just cut a device company's revenue by 8% in a quarter. The reimbursement lever for medtech isn't price, it's friction. $INSP
items.tweetB: Vertex, Inspire, Henry Schein: healthcare reported beats and sold off anyway. The common thread is cost and access, not demand.

items.title: Silence from founders is 'a 100% accurate predictor of death' (PG), but one in five investors reply to a monthly update
items.idea: A Notion Capital investor reviewed real investor updates: Paubox's Hoala Greevy has sent one monthly since Dec 2016; Shoelace's MRR went from $2,230 to $32,726 over 13 updates; Kapwing's Julia Enthoven got a reply from roughly one in five investors and an answer to an ask from another one in five. Kleiner's Mamoon Hamid says a good early-stage update takes under two minutes to read. Deel's Bouaziz stopped monthly updates once investors stopped helping.
items.angle: Information asymmetry between founders and investors is a data point: update cadence is a leading indicator of survival. Useful as a venture-diligence filter.
items.tweetA: Shoelace's MRR went from $2,230 to $32,726 across 13 monthly updates. The updates didn't cause the growth, but the habit that wrote them probably did. Cadence is a diligence signal.
items.tweetB: One in five investors reply to a founder's update and another one in five do something about the ask. If you're not asking, you're leaving a 20% hit rate on the table.
